Buying a fund just before its year-end distribution: what it really costs in a non-registered account

A distribution paid days after you buy hands part of your own money back as taxable income. Follow the same purchase made just before and just after the distribution: identical units and value, a higher cost base, tax paid now and partly won back later. See how the cost depends on distribution size, its tax character and how long you hold.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Buy a non-registered fund just before its distribution, or just after?

Interactive planning lab

Distribution paid on the new units$1,600
Tax due this year if you buy just before$296.5
Higher cost base from the reinvested distribution$1,600
Capital-gains tax saved at the sale in year 10$237.2
Net cost of buying before, in year-10 dollars$142.35
Same net cost in today’s dollars$111.2
Share of this year’s tax won back at the sale (today’s dollars)62.50%

$20,000 buys units in a non-registered account either just before or just after a distribution of 8% of the unit price. Bought before, the $1,600 distribution is reinvested, so both buyers end up with the same units and the same market value; the difference is tax. 75% of the distribution is treated as capital gains (half taxed) and the rest as income taxed in full at 29.65%, a conservative simplification: eligible dividends would be taxed less and return of capital is not taxed now. That tax is paid from cash that would otherwise earn 2.5% after tax. Units grow 5% a year and are all sold in year 10. In a TFSA, RRSP or other registered plan none of this tax arises. Figures are hypothetical, not a forecast or a personal tax calculation.

The central idea

Buying a fund in a taxable account just before a distribution does not lose you any investment value, but it pulls tax forward. The cost base rises by the distribution, so part of that tax comes back when you sell. The lasting cost is the growth on the tax cash and, if the distribution is income rather than capital gains, the difference in tax rates. It is usually modest, it is zero in a TFSA or RRSP, and it is rarely worth staying out of the market for long to avoid.

01

A December purchase and a February tax slip

Many mutual funds and ETFs pay most of their yearly distribution in December, especially the capital gains the fund realized during the year. Someone who invests a bonus or a year-end lump sum in a non-registered account in mid-December may find, a few days later, that the fund has paid a distribution, the unit price has dropped by about the same amount, and a tax slip is on the way for income they feel they never earned.

That feeling is correct in one sense. The distribution is not new profit for the buyer: it is a slice of their own purchase money handed back. But CRA taxes it like any other distribution. This guide puts numbers on the trade-off. The tool compares buying just before the distribution with buying just after, using the same amount of money, and follows both until the units are sold.

The question only exists in a non-registered (taxable) account. Inside a TFSA, RRSP, RRIF, RESP or FHSA, distributions are not taxed in the year they are paid, so the date of purchase relative to a distribution makes no tax difference there.

02

Why the distribution is your own money coming back

A fund’s unit price is its net asset value per unit. When the fund pays a distribution, that cash leaves the fund, so the unit price falls by the distribution, all else being equal. With the defaults, $20,000 buys units just before a distribution of 8% of the price. The distribution is $1,600 and the units are then worth $18,400. Reinvested at the lower price, the $1,600 buys more units, and the holding is back to $20,000.

Someone who waits and buys just after the distribution pays the lower price for the same $20,000 and ends up with exactly the same number of units. The first chart shows the result: equal market value, but a different adjusted cost base and a different tax bill this year.

CRA’s guidance on mutual funds explains why. Distributions are taxed while you own the units, and if you reinvest them you must still report them, because you are considered to have received them before reinvesting. Reinvesting buys more units, which raises your average cost per unit. The early buyer’s cost base is $21,600 against the later buyer’s $20,000. That higher cost base is the record of the tax already paid.

03

The character of the distribution sets the first bill

A fund distribution can be capital gains, Canadian dividends, foreign income, interest, other income or return of capital, or a mix, and the T3 or T5 slip says which. Each is taxed differently. Capital gains are half included in income. Interest and foreign income are fully taxed. Eligible Canadian dividends get the gross-up and dividend tax credit. Return of capital is not taxed now; it lowers the cost base instead.

The tool splits the distribution into a capital-gains part and an “everything else” part, and taxes the second at the full marginal rate. That is conservative for dividends and wrong for return of capital, which would cost nothing now. With 75% capital gains and a 29.65% rate, the $1,600 distribution brings $296.50 of tax: $177.90 on the capital-gains part and $118.60 on the rest. Year-end distributions of equity funds are often mostly capital gains; bond and balanced funds pay more interest through the year.

The fund income-type guide compares these characters in detail, and the return-of-capital guide shows how a non-taxable distribution works in the other direction.

04

Chart 2: part of the tax comes back when you sell

Because the early buyer’s cost base is $1,600 higher, their capital gain on sale is $1,600 smaller. At half inclusion and 29.65%, that saves $237.20 of tax in the year of sale, whatever the sale price. If the units are sold for less than cost, the same $1,600 enlarges a capital loss instead.

So the tax is not doubled; it is moved. The cost is in three places. First, the tax is paid now rather than years later, and the cash used to pay it cannot grow in the meantime. Second, the income part of the distribution was taxed in full, but it is recovered only through a capital gain that is half taxed: in the default, $118.60 paid on income comes back as $59.30 at sale. Third, the early buyer needs cash for the tax this year.

The second chart shows the net cost by the year of sale. A sale right after the distribution leaves a net cost of $59.30, the tax-rate difference alone. After 10 years, with the tax cash earning 2.5% after tax, the net cost is about $142 in year-10 dollars, or about $111 in today’s dollars, roughly 0.56% of the $20,000 invested. In today’s dollars about 62% of the first-year tax is won back.

05

Chart 3: where the cost comes from

The waterfall breaks the year-10 cost into its parts: $177.90 of tax on the capital-gains part, $118.60 on the income part, $83.05 of growth forgone on that $296.50, less the $237.20 of capital-gains tax saved at the sale. The total is $142.35.

Read it as a timing cost, not a loss of investment value. Both buyers own the same units throughout, and the after-tax value of the early buyer’s holding, net of the tax already paid, trails the later buyer’s by only that amount. A large fall in the market a few weeks after either purchase would matter far more than this difference.

The cost rises with the size of the distribution, the share taxed as income, your marginal rate and the length of time before you sell. It falls if the distribution is mostly return of capital, if you are in a low bracket this year and expect a higher one later, or if you were going to sell soon anyway.

06

Chart 4: distribution size and holding period

The heatmap scales the result to $10,000 invested and varies the distribution from 2% to 16% of the unit price and the year of sale from 1 to 30. With the other defaults, a 2% distribution costs about $8 to $23 in today’s dollars per $10,000; an 8% distribution about $33 to $92; an unusually large 16% distribution about $65 to $183.

Large year-end distributions usually come from funds that sold appreciated holdings during the year, for example after a strong market, a manager change or heavy redemptions by other investors. Fund companies often publish estimated year-end distributions in November or early December, with a record date that decides who receives them. Checking the estimate before a large December purchase is cheap; the actual amount and its character are confirmed only on the tax slip.

A fund that distributes little and grows mostly through unrealized gains defers tax for its holders in general, which is one reason fund turnover and distribution history matter for non-registered accounts beyond the December question.

07

Should you wait until after the distribution?

  1. Inside a registered account, ignore it. In a TFSA, RRSP, RRIF, RESP or FHSA the distribution is not taxed when paid. The account’s rules, not the fund, decide that: a fund is not tax-exempt in itself.
  2. In a taxable account, compare a few days with the cost. If the record date is days away and the estimated distribution is large, waiting for it to pass is a reasonable, low-cost habit. Waiting weeks or months to save a cost of this size is market timing, and missing a rise could easily cost more; the waiting-for-a-dip guide shows how cash rules drift.
  3. Keep the cost base records. Reinvested distributions raise your adjusted cost base. Many platforms track it, but CRA expects you to calculate it for each fund and series. Missing the reinvested amounts means paying tax twice on the same money when you sell.
  4. Keep the cash for the tax. A reinvested distribution produces no cash. The tax cash provision guide shows how to set money aside for it.
  5. Do not let tax drive the choice of fund. Diversification, fees, risk and the time until you need the money matter more than one distribution. Returns are uncertain; a fund bought after its distribution can still fall.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 26 October 2026. The tax treatment of fund distributions, reinvested distributions and the adjusted cost base is from CRA pages reviewed 26 October 2026. The 29.65% default is the 2026 federal 20.5% plus Ontario 9.15% bracket rates from CRA’s 2026 rate page. Purchase size, distribution, growth and cash return are hypothetical editable inputs, not the record of any fund or a personal tax calculation. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Canada Revenue Agency · Tax treatment of mutual funds ↗

    Reviewed in the in-app browser on 26 October 2026: distributions are taxed while units are owned and must be reported even when reinvested; distributions can be capital gains, dividends, foreign income, interest, other income or return of capital; reinvesting distributions changes the average cost per unit; return of capital reduces the ACB; mutual funds held in a TFSA or tax-deferred plans are outside the section.

  2. Canada Revenue Agency · Calculating and reporting your capital gains and losses ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026 for the adjusted cost base definition and the 1/2 inclusion rate referenced on the page.

  3. Canada Revenue Agency · Current year tax rates and income brackets (2026) ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026 by an earlier TickerLantern guide: federal 20.5% from CAD 58,523 to CAD 117,045 and Ontario 9.15% from CAD 53,891 to CAD 107,785, giving the 29.65% default combined rate. Your own rate depends on your province and income.
